cards.note: Within Assam, you can find corn between Guwahati and Nagaon, south of the river.
Within Assam, sugarcane is mainly found around Lanka
Within Bihar, tea plantations can be found in the far Northeast.
Canola is mostly found in and around Rajasthan.
Cotton is commonly found in the western parts of India, particularly in Gujarat and Maharashtra.
Maharashtra is by far the state with the highest grape production in India.
Within Madhya Pradesh, sugar cane can commonly be found southwest and northeast of the Satpura National Park.

Cotton (within) is mostly found around Nanded, more generally in the middle/eastern part of Maharashtra.

Note by MB: Very unreliable in my experience
Sugarcane in Maharashtra is mostly central from what I saw.
Oil palm plantations are almost exclusive to Andhra Pradesh and are mostly located around Eluru.
Pineapple is very uncommon in India, but if you see it, it's in Bihar in the corridor between Nepal and Bangladesh.
Sugarcane is most commonly found in the north in and around Uttar Pradesh, and in the southwest.

Sugar cane can be found in several areas, the two main ones being near Erode and Thiruvanamalai.

It is also findable in smaller areas between those two big areas, but it is still mainly a northern Tamil Nadu thing.
Within Assam, Tea is mostly planted in the eastern and in the southern regions. There are also some patches in Western Assam.
Tea plantations in India are mostly located in the northeast and in Kerala, but it spills in one particular area in Tamil Nadu northwest of Coimbatore
Within Tripura, Tea is found along the Bangladeshi border, and along the Assamese border.
Within West Bengal, tea plantations are found near the northern border to Bhutan.

Tea plantations can be found in the northeast and the far south.

NOTE: If you find tea plantations in a flat area, you are likely in Assam or northeastern West Bengal, near the Assam border.

Cotton fields in Telangana are logically next to the big area that produces the most of it in Maharashtra, so it is gonna be found mostly north-west of the state. You can click in Nizamabad for a good score.

Note by MB: In my experience, it's more common North of Nizamabad.

Within Andhra Pradesh, thatched roofs can commonly be found in three places.

  • Mainly south east of Guntur
  • Secondarily south of Nellore, where a rare red car can be found.
  • Sparsely around Srikakulam
Within Assam, you can find thatched roofs all the way north east in the state.
In Assam, you can find houses with woven walls along the border to Arunachal Pradesh, north of Tinsukia.
If you see these hip roofs made out of tin - which are usually found in West Bengal - in Bihar, you're in the Northeastern Quarter of Bihar.

Within Bihar, you can find regular Wide W Tiles around Katihar.

Reminder: This type of tile is like a larger kind of W tile. Another way to tell it apart is the small pike in the middle of the tile.
Houses with tiled roofs and blue painted walls are very common in Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh, a little less in Madhya Pradesh

In poorer parts of the Ganges Valley it is common for villages to construct their own large chimneys to fire clay into bricks. These can be seen from far away and are a good clue for the Ganges Valley specifically, especially UP and Bihar. Note that they are also fairly common in the poorer eastern parts of Tamil Nadu.
Houses made out of clay are most common in Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand. There's some spill in far southwestern Bihar.
Clay houses exist a lot in Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand, and some spill can be seen in southwestern Bihar.
White painted clay huts are found in northwestern Bihar, northwest of Muzaffapur.
Houses with colorful, particularly blue painted walls, can be found in the areas around Eastern Madhya, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand.
Large hip roofs made of corrugated sheet metal are found in West Bengal and adjacent areas in Bihar and Odisha.

- Shorter and "pyramidal" towers (Vimana) - most easily recognizable

  • Monumental and ornate gate (Gopuram)
  • Door Guardian Statues (Dvarapala)

Found in the South of India.
Houses between Dumka and Pakur have long tiled roofs and walls are painted in two colors (green/blue with an orange/brown color at the bottom

Found mostly in the main, southern part of West Bengal, but more in the west. Sometimes also found in Bihar at the border to eastern Nepal.

Note by MB: This meta is not sufficiently researched, but it's still good to know
Flat Guna tiles is just a tiled roof full of staple-shaped tiles. It can be found around Prayagraj, south east of the state.
Flat tiles seem to be the worst type of tile by their appearance. They are mainly found in Madhya Pradesh and southern Uttar pradesh.

It has a “U” shape but there is a flatter shaped tile connecting tiles to each other.

It’s very common in southeastern Uttar Pradesh, western Bihar and rarely in northeastern Madhya Pradesh and Jharkhand.
Houses in Odisha are often painted green.
These huts that are made entirely out of hay, and have thatched roofs are found in Southwestern Bihar, mainly between Patna and Gaya.

Jammu looks like a fairly developed state compared to most places in India. The architecture looks richer and overall way nicer. Punjab has a similar architecture.

50/50 Tip ! It can be hard to differentiate Punjab and Jammu in urban rounds due to the similarity of their architecture. If you see rich looking houses, look at the car to know whether you are in Punjab or in Jammu. If you don’t see one of the two Jammu cars (boxy with top right thread or central strap, see image 3&4), click Punjab.

Note by MB: This 50/50 tip is not 100% reliable, so look at other clues (like Punjabi language) too.
In the eastern parts of Jharkhand, you can find some West Bengal wide W tiles spill
Flat tiles can be spotted in random places in Madhya Pradesh, but mainly around Guna, Chhatarpur and Sagar in the center of the state.
Slate roofs in Madhya Pradesh can be found west of Sagar
U tiles are more common in the eastern half of Madhya Pradesh.
W tiles are quite rare in Madhya Pradesh but can still be seen west of Jabalpur and south of Guna
Nallukettu architecture has distinct roofs, which are often very high and red. This style is often found around Kerala Backwaters.

Thatched roofs can be found pretty much all over the eastern coast of India. In the state of Odisha, they can mostly be seen between Balasore and Puri, but also more inland and in the southwest of the state.

If you see only thatched, the coast is more likely.
U tiles are commonly found on the northwest of the state, on the borders with Jharkhand and Chhattsgarh.
When mixed with thatched roofs, U Tiles are most commonly found around Umerkote.

W tiled roofs can be found in two areas in Odisha:

  • corridor north of Bhubaneswar
  • Southwestern Odisha, southwest of Bhawanipatna

W tiled roofs combined with Thatched Roofs can be found in two areas in Odisha:

  • corridor north of Bhubaneswar
  • Southwestern Odisha, southwest of Bhawanipatna

Note by MB: This is also true if you just see W-Tiles, without Thatched Roofs.
When mixed with W-Tiles, U-Tiles are most commonly found around Umerkote.

If you see orange/black wide W tiles, you're probably around Madhubani (BR).

Reminder: This type of tile is like a larger kind of W tile. Another way to tell it apart is the small pike in the middle of the tile.
Woven walls, plastered with clay are found on the western half of the Bihar-Nepal border.
While Red Brick can be found anywhere in India, there is a notable concentration in the Ganges River Valley, especially towards the West.

Shimla is definitely the place in the Himalayas with the biggest amount of bright green and bright red roofs (and architecture in general).

Note by MB: It also spams Himalayan Cedars.

Gurdwaras, which can typically be recognised by their white domes and ornate walls, are most common in Punjab. You can also sometimes recognise them by the Sikh Khanda symbol, which represents the religion.
Roofs in Sikkim often have this short "curtain" hanging down on the side of the roof.

Slate roofs can be found in a very specific area between Kalaburagi and Hyderabad in Telangana.

Note by MB: This is the same area where they use the thin grey stones (see thin grey stones meta), and thus you can often see them in combination
Houses made of square panels separated by thin beams are found in Northeast India, mainly in Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur.
Wooden huts with sticks around can be found in the western half of Bihar, at a latitude between Patna and Muzaffarpur..
Houses with very "strong colors", such as dark yellow, pink, purple, are often found in Tamil Nadu, and sometimes in Kerala and Andhra Pradesh

In Tamil Nadu, you will often come across quite good looking houses, the most recognizable are the ones with W tiled roofs and blueish paint. The combination of the color and the tiles should be 95% Tamil Nadu, the remaining 5% being spill in bordering states.

W tiled roofs are pretty much everywhere but somewhat less common in the northeast and on the eastern coast, where U tiles can be found more commonly.

Houses or huts with thatched roofs are mainly found along the east coast and northern plains. Large hay mounds are also generally more common in this region. Thatched roofs from Uttar Pradesh to Odisha tend to be made of fine pieces of hay.

Houses or huts with thatched roofs are mainly found along the east coast and northern plains. Large hay mounds are also generally more common in this region. Thatched roofs from Odisha to Tamil Nadu tend to be made of dried palm fans.
In Tamil Nadu, thatched roofs are more common south east of Thanjavur.

The area on the border of Telangana and Karnataka often have houses with roofs made out of distinctly thin grey bricks. These grey bricks and similar coloured rocks are sometimes also seen in walls and scattered on the ground in stockyards.
Metal roofs, with a small triangle near the top, are common in Northeast India.

These rounded tiles are found mostly in

  • Chhattisgarh
  • Jharkhand
  • Bihar
  • Eastern Madhya

You can also find them in

  • Eastern Gujarat
  • Eastern Tamil Nadu
  • North-Western Telangana

U tiled roofs are quite rare in Tamil Nadu, but if you come across such roofs, it should be in the northeast.

It is possible to find some further down near Thanjavur, but it will more likely come with the combination of thatched roofs.
W-Tiles are mostly found on the western coast and in Tamil Nadu, but it also goes further inland in western Madhya Pradesh and in Telangana.
If you come across a W tiled roof in Karnataka, you can basically go in the western/southwestern part

The only type of tile in Telangana is the W tile type.

As you can see, it doesn’t go in the south of the state.
Goa and Kerala are two of the most developed states in India and often have very wealthy and modern homes.
In West Bengal, houses with walls painted in two colors (green/blue with an orange/brown color at the bottom, are usually found near the Jharkhand border.

This type of tile is like a larger kind of W tile. Another way to tell it apart is the small pike in the middle of the tile.

It is very common in West Bengal, eastern Jharkhand and eastern Bihar, but doesn’t go further north than Purnia, Bihar.

The coverage on road NH326 (labelled 326) west of Brahmapur in Odisha has a thin grey antenna. The images are generally very high-quality for shitcam, with an especially high quality near the Harabhangi Reservoir.
This car has a back curving bar, but is mostly blurred. It can be found east of Kuno National Park
This is the most common, though not only car on Andaman.

cards.a: Car Meta - Arunachal Pradesh - Back Antenna
cards.note: Within Arunachal Pradesh, a back antenna can be found around Chowkam and East of Namsai.

cards.a: Car Meta - Arunachal Pradesh - White Car with Mirrors

If you see a back antenna in Assam, you're in the far east of the state.

This is not something you will come across very often, but if you have a black car and don’t really know where to go/want to confirm your guess, black car is more common in Telangana/Andhra Pradesh, especially in Northern Telangana and Coastal AP.
This black car, uniquely characterized through the black bars on each the side, is only found in Goa.

Large visible, square shaped cars can be found in all states northwest of Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh, except for Madhya Pradesh. It can also be found in and around Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Chennai.
A boxy car with 5 indents can be found near the river mouth of the Subarnarekha river near the Odisha/WB border.
A boxy car with 6 indents is found near Malkangiri, Odisha.
Boxy car in Karnataka is only found in and around Bengaluru.
A boxy car with an extra step at the front is found in Odisha.
A car with flowers on the front can be found around Keonjhar, on the 49 and the 20.
This car (note the antenna!) can be found in Goa, and in the Union Territory of Daman.
This car is unique to Haryal, PB. It looks similar to the boxy car, but with a rounded front.

cards.a: Car Meta - Himachal Pradesh - Boxy Car
cards.note: Shimla is the only city in Himachal Pradesh to have a boxy car, which is this car with the top right corner visible with a thread (sometimes not visible).

White car, box car with bars and the central strap leaning right.

It can be found mainly in Jammu/Kashmir but sometimes in Sultanpur, UP.
All roads in Ladakh have this white car with visible front.

The "Adidas Car" is characterized by the black stripes on the white car front. Sometimes it has a visible side mirror. It also often has a visible bar at the back.

It is exclusive to the island of Amini

A big circular blur (either full blurred or transparently blurred) is very common in Retrocam. On Lakshadweep, however, it is only found on Andrott and Kalpeni (both also have a car that's unique for these islands respectively).

cards.a: Car Meta - Lakshadweep - Blurred Black Front
cards.note:
This car with the subtle black blur at the front is found in Kalpeni. The blur can be very subtle sometimes, and is confusable with the blurred white edges on Agatti.

Sometimes the same car has a slightly different blur, where the edges are exposed.

Kalpeni can also have a big circular blur, so don't rule out Kalpeni if you don't see this car.

cards.a: Car Meta - Lakshadweep - Blurred White Edges
cards.note: This car is mostly blurred and has subtle white edges at the front. It's found on the island of Agatti. Sometimes the edges are so subtle that you can overlook them and confuse it with the Kalpeni car (which has a subtle black blur)
This car with an exposed black front is unique to Kiltan. Note that the front is always exposed on Kiltan, if it's blurred (even partly), it's not the Kiltan car.

The red front blur can be found on Andrott. Sometimes, the same car has a bit different blur, where there's some exposed red visible.

Note that Andrott can also have the big circular blur where you see no car.

cards.a: Car Meta - Lakshadweep - White Car with Mirror
cards.note: This car is the most likely to encounter if you get Lakshadweep. It has a white front and always a bit of mirror visible on the left. Sometimes a part of the mirror is blurred, but you can always see at least a bit of it exposed. This car is so common because it's on the main island of Lakshadweep, Kavaratti.

cards.a: Car Meta - Lakshadweep - White Exposed Front
cards.note: This car with an exposed white front is found of Kadmat. This car can be confused with others: It's not the Kadmat car if it has a visible side mirror. It's also not the Kadmat car if the front is blurred.
Mechuka features a unique car in Arunachal. It can be found in the valley and on the road leading to it from Along on the NH13.

cards.a: Car Meta - Mizoram - Double Mirror Car
cards.note: In Mizoram, a grey car with double mirrors appears in the southernmost coverage, near the NH502.

If you see a long antenna, combined with a black car front in Mizoram, you're on the NH6 north of Serkhan.

Keep in mind this car is not unique to Mizoram.
A car with a black front and a stubby antenna within Mizoram can be found on the roads west of Aizawi.
This car has an antenna with some kind of a spring. It basically goes from Salem to Chennai.
In the eastern parts of Ajmer, RJ, you can sometimes see an open trunk in Smallcam. It can be found north of Shrinagar/west of Circular Rd.
A car with an orange flag can be found in the Jharkhand north-east panhandle.

cards.a: Car Meta - Punjab - Black Boxy Car
cards.note: Within Punjab, the black boxy car can be found on the Pakistani border between Firozpur and Amritsar.

cards.a: Car Meta - Punjab - Dasuya Forest Car
cards.note: Within Punjab, this car is is unique to Dasuya Forest. Beware that this car is not unique to Punjab though.

cards.a: Car Meta - Punjab - Red Boxy Car
cards.note: Within Punjab, the red boxy car can be found in Ludhiana, Chandigarh, and a bit north between them. The coverage forms a reverse 'v'.
This cool car with a spoiler at the back can be found in Max-North Andaman, near Daglipur.
This car has a back curving bar at the front and white bars on the side. It's found mostly around Rewa, but also around Raipura.
Within Arunachal Pradesh, both this black and this red car are exclusively found in Roing. The black car appears mainly on the NH313 and east. The red car appears mainly west of the main road.

cards.a: Car Meta - Satpura National Park Car
cards.note: This car has a back-curving bar and a singular black bar. It's found mainly east of Satpura National Park, and sometimes around Raipura.
If you see this white, boxy-looking car in Arunachal Pradesh, you're on the road between Tezu and Lohitpur.

In the very far western part of the Meghalaya, on the roads north of Purakhasia, you can find a particular car with an antenna on the top left. It can be quite hard to see so be aware it exists so you know what to look for

cards.a: Car Meta - White Goa Car with bar
cards.note: This white car, uniquely characterized through the bar on the side, which is black and grey, is only found in Goa.

While the car is blurred most of the time, Sikkim features a noticeable car that gives the western part of Sikkim, starting at Rangpo.

It can have an antenna, be blurred, almost invisible, but as long as you see a yellow car, you know it’s here.

Andaman Islands are remote Islands that have their own distinct vegetation. It is covered in areca palm forests and the roads are often very thin.

Andaman has been covered using a camera with maxed out saturation somehow. The result is these very bright/white colors.

In 2025, a large part of the NH-66 in Kerala is under construction, making it very recognizable.

If you see a long, straight highway with construction in Smallcam, you're likely to be on the NH-66.
Many locations in Tripura have a pretty low brightness, despite the sun being out and not setting.
This double smudge can be found in the central-northern parts of the Yawal Wildlife Sanctuary in Madhya Pradesh.

Poles in Madhya Pradesh often have a metal bar shaped like an upside down A (∀) slightly below the top of the pole.

94% Madhya Pradesh 2% Jharkhand 1% each: Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu
Poles with two diagonal bars forming a ‘<’ shape are common in Meghalaya (75%) and Arunachal Pradesh (20%) and occasionally found in Assam (2%).
This pole configuraiton is mainly found in Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh.
Found everywhere except for North-East.
Commonly found everywhere, except for North East. Within North-East, it is sometimes found in Assam.

These black paint can be circular or square, features 2 letters, an arrow beneath, and some numbers beneath that and can be on metal/concrete poles.

They're found mostly near the capital (Port Blair/Sri Vijaya Puram) (95%) and rarely near Diglipur (5%)
Pole tops in Andaman mostly consist of horizontal bars perpendicular to the pole. They are not 100% unique to Andaman, but are very common there.
This black-yellow-black pole painting (which is famous for appearing in Antioquia in Colo), can also be found in Eastern Bihar along the Ganges.

A section of the NH13 west of Roing has poles marked with white numbers on blue, red or black paint.
These vans (can be white, red, or orange) with specifically yellow plates, in NE India are found only within West Bengal and Assam. Doesn’t count with a white plate.
Many roads in Assam are paved with these tiles. What makes it stand out is that it is also found on very rural roads.
Trident poletops with the tip of the middle bar bent at a 90° angle can be found in Assam (98%).

Bangur Cement is found in large parts of India.

  • Gujarat

Pole paint consisting of exactly four thicker black and yellow stripes can be found in Bihar.

In Bihar and Jharkhand you will see many ads with this man with a turban and a beard. He's usually accompanied by a hexagonal company logo and a yellow background.

Black Tuk-Tuks are most common in Maharashtra (maybe fake meta)
The bridges in West Bengal frequently feature blue and white concrete blocks. It is also rarely found in Bihar around the city of Gaya.

Buddhist prayer flags and other Buddhist signals are mostly found in the Himalayas. Sometimes you can also find them in the Northeast, around Bangladesh, especially in Western Meghalaya, Western Mizoram and Southern Tripura. Rarely you can find it in central-eastern Maharashtra around Nagpur.

NOTE: The nearby cities of Sahibzada Ajit Singh Nagar and Panchkula are also planned industrial cities, which feature somewhat similar signs.

The City of Chandigarh is a planned industrial city. As a result, the city features a lot of unique infrastructure, such as blue signs mentioning sectors and industrial areas.

NOTE: The nearby cities of Sahibzada Ajit Singh Nagar and Panchkula are also planned industrial cities, which feature somewhat similar signs.

The City of Chandigarh is a planned industrial city. As a result, the city features a lot of unique infrastructure, such as street signs which will typically feature several numbers rather than street names.

NOTE: The nearby cities of Sahibzada Ajit Singh Nagar and Panchkula are also planned industrial cities, which feature somewhat similar signs.

Trident poletop, V-shaped bars underneath and Punjab Poletop.

The western parts of Rajasthan can commonly be recognised by the dry landscape with sandy soil.

Unique hilly landscape with dead trees. Note that not all coverage in this park looks like this.
Assamese, mainly found in Assam, also uses the Bengali script, with the addition of some characters, most notably ৰ and ৱ.

Bengali is found in northeastern India and has a similar look to Devanagari (Hindi), however it can usually be recognised by the many letters featuring left-facing triangular shapes.

NOTE: This is also the language found in Bangladesh.

Hindi is the most common language in India and can be found in many central and northern regions. It uses the Devanagari script, which can be recognised by the line going through the top of each word and the straight vertical lines found in the majority of all letters.

Note by MB: Maharashtra has a different language that uses the same script.
Gujarati, found in Gujarat, has a script with several similarities to the Hindi script, however it notably lacks the horizontal line at the top of every word.

Kannada is found in Karnataka and has a script with a lot of smooth curves and small circles. It is very similar to the Telugu script, with Telugu having one additional feature described in the next tip. Many characters also feature a distinct squiggly tail in the top right corner, which is less common in Telugu.
The Malayalam script can be found in Kerala and mostly consists of somewhat simple-looking curvy letters, often containing upside-down U-shapes.

Marathi, found in Maharashtra, also uses the Devanagari script, however it sometimes uses the letter ळ which is not found in Hindi.

Further differences, analyzed by MB:

  • Vowels with this symbol on top (ऍ) are exclusive to Marathi
  • Marathi uses Western Full Stops '.' , while Hindi uses Devanagari full stops '।'
  • This letter: ण is more common in Marathi (but not exclusive)
  • Marathi does NOT use those dots (nukta) on the bottom left of a character: ज़
Manipuri, also called Meitei, is the official language of Manipur. It is written using the Meitei script, which can be recognised by its many vertical lines and right angles.
Mizo, found in Mizoram, is the language most commonly found on the Indian coverage other than English, which uses the Latin script.
The state of Meghalaya uses English primarily and no other scripts. Thus if you see a lot of signs and no non-english language, you are most likely in Meghalaya.

The Oriya script is found in Odisha and has a curvy look, with many letters having wide semi-circles covering the top. Many letters have a distinct diacritic in the shape of a wide curve above the top of the letter. A useful mnemonic is that the shape of the characters resembles a skull emoji .

Punjabi can be found in Punjab in northwestern India. While the script looks somewhat similar to Hindi, it can generally be differentiated by the softer shape of the letters and the horizontal bar being broken over certain letters. It also has some distinctly different features, such as the letters ਨ, ਲ and ਅ as well as a diacritic in the shape of a soft curve beneath a letter.

The Tamil script is found in Tamil Nadu and has a distinct combination of curves, straight lines and 90° angles. Some letters also have diacritics shaped like dots.

NOTE: Tamil is also commonly found in Sri Lanka.
Telugu, found in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, has a script very similar to Kannada, but you’ll often see diacritics resembling checkmarks at the top of letters.

Their flag is rarely shown, but you can often find Karbi colors (dark red, black and white) in those districts.
This is an unofficial flag of Karnataka.
Flag of a political party active only in Tamil Nadu
People wearing a Lungi, which looks like a towel wrapped around the waist, are more common in South India.
Flag of a political party only active in Tamil Nadu.
The Meitei people inhabit Manipur state, especially Imphal. Their flag is commonly found in and around that city.

Flag of a political party only active in Tamil Nadu.

The tiger symbol can sometimes be found without the flag.
This blue flag with this symbol in the middle is specific for Navayana Buddhism, the branch of Buddhism common in Central-Eastern Maharashtra.
This shell is the symbol of a Odisha specific political party: Biju Janata Dal
Exclusive to Uttar Pradesh, their symbol is a bicycle.
This flag and this symbol stand for Sarnaism. They are very localized, found in Ranchi and in Southern Jharkhand.
People wearing colorful scarfs are generally found in the north of India.
Shivaji is a person often depicted on statues in Maharashtra. He is always riding a horse, and is often accompanied by an orange flag.
This party has an orange-red-green flag and a table lamp as a symbol. It operates exclusively in Sikkim.

The flag of this party often has these flowers on some grass with the Indian flag as background.

It can be found mainly in West Bengal, however less commonly in the Northern Parts. Sometimes it's also found in Western Meghalaya

Tripra Mothi is a Tripura-specific party. Its flag has two vertical stripes, yellow and red.

Don't confuse it with the Karnataka flag, where the stripes are horizontal.

The flag of UPPL is yellow white green with a farmer on a tractor on it. Found in Bodoland, which consists of the Assamese districts bordering Bhutan.

Don't confuse this with the Gorkha seperatist flag, which is green-white-yellow.
Blue and red flag with a Myanmar-style star, found only in Tamil Nadu.
This party is exclusive to Andhra Pradesh, and most popular in the South. Their symbol is a ceiling fan.

Agaves are mostly found in Karnataka

Note by MB: This is generally a fake meta, Agaves can be found in many different places throughout India. But if you have really nothing else to go off, Karnataka is definitely a place to conside.r

Areca Palms can be recognised by their very thin trunk and a small crown.

They are most common in Assam, but also in other northeastern areas, stretiching to coastal Odisha. A second common region is Kerala and coastal Karnataka
In Assam, these white flowers can often be seen along the road in three areas: - The border to West Bengal - The border to Eastern Bhutan - West of Nagaon.

Recognition (most visible when you look at the bottom of the crown):

  • symmetrical pattern of needles on twigs
  • thin twigs
  • twigs draping down

Found in:

  • mostly Western Sikkim and Sangti, Manda La, Salari (Arunachal Pradesh)
  • often in Khellong, Rupa (Arunachal Pradesh)
  • sometimes Rest of Sikkim, and Arunachal, west of Jamiri
  • rarely in West Bengal near Sikkim Border.

Recognition:

  • whiteish-greyish tinge
  • Short needles
  • long slender cones
  • two rows of hanging needles
  • many branches, little space between them

Found in:

  • Max West Arunachal, Mechuka
  • sometimes Ziro, Neora Valley National Park (West Bengal)
  • very rarely Sikkim

Recognition:

  • individual branches well visible
  • edges of branches have thin brush of new needles
  • in higher elevation, the crown will be conical
  • needles drape down in all directions

Found in:

  • mostly: Max West Arunachal; Road south of Harsil
  • sometimes: Dharamshala, Manali, Kullu, Shimla, Sarahan, Southern Uttarakhand Mountains
  • rarely: Further inside the Uttarakhand mountains
Calotropis Procera is found all over Rajasthan and less in surrounding states so it is a good clue for Rajasthan if you have a lot of it.

Recognition

  • round crown
  • young pines: conical crown, thick brush for new needles Found in
  • Mountainous Uttarakhand; Shimla, Dalhousie (Himachal Pradesh); Elevated Jammu / Kashmir
  • Sometimes Dharamshala (Himachal Pradesh)
  • Rarely low elevation dry valleys in Western Arunachal Pradesh

Coconut palms are most common in Kerala, the Western Half of Karnataka and Southern Coastal Maharashtra In general, they appear near Coasts, near the border to Bangladesh, and anywhere South of Central Telangana

cards.a: Vegetation - Combination of Date Palm & Palmyra Palm
cards.note: In Jharkhand, you will very often see the combination of date palms (a lot of them) and palmyra palms. I think it is one of the best clues for getting Jharkhand because it’s pretty unique. I also saw a lot of that combination of palms in Telangana so be careful and look for text before guessing.
Date palms can be found in Central India. They appear North of the Latitude of Chhattisgarh, except for Himalayan states, the Northeast and Western Gujarat/RJ.
Within Tamil Nadu, date palms can be found in the North-East.
These 'dead'-looking trees are a very strong point to go to Rajasthan. They are concentrated mostly southwest of Sikar.
Doum palms, which appear similar to Palmyra palms but with multiple branches, are almost exclusive to the union territory of Diu.
Eucalyptus trees are a good clue for the Uttarakhand foothills and nearby areas in Uttar Pradesh.
This type of cacti (Euphorbia neriifolia) can commonly be seen as part of fences throughout Gujarat, western Maharashtra and the southern half of Rajasthan.
South of Udaipur, you can find a very distinct landscape with narrow hills and a lot of this type of cactus (Euphorbia).

Recognition:

  • downward bending branches
  • very short needles

Found in

  • Shimla, Dalhousie, Dharamshala, Palampur, Kasol, Jibhi, South of Kullu, South of Manali (HP); Road from Harsil to Gangotri (UK) and Southwestern UK in general
  • sometimes in Kangra, Solan, Manali-Dalang road (HP) and around Rudrapayag (UK)
  • rarely in eastern Uttarakhand

Recognition:

  • twig with two symmetrical rows of short needles
  • downward bending twigs
  • crowns look a bit disorganized

Found in:

  • South of Senge and South of Dirang (Western Arunachal Pradesh)
The endangered Indian pitcher plant is exclusive to the Khasi Hills, which are mainly in Meghalaya. They can occasionally be spotted on road sides, especially on the NH206 north of Umlārem.

This tree, often called Jand by Indians, can be recognized by the clusters of leaves at the end of thick branches.

It is found in Northern Rajasthan and Southern Haryana/Punjab.

Recognition:

  • puffy, conical crown
  • smooth reddish bark with parallel vertical indents
  • "sea grass twigs" (look at picture #3)
  • twigs growing in all directions

Found in:

  • Sikkim/WB Border
  • Meghalaya Hills
  • Dirang, Khellong, Bomdila (Arunachal)
  • sometimes more north in Sikkim and west of Jamiri (Arunachal)
  • rarely east of Jamiri (AR)

Recognition:

  • disorganized crowns, neither conical nor round
  • younger pines can appear round, but have shorter needles

Found in:

  • Meghalaya Hills
  • Raga & South of Ziro Junction (Arunachal Pradesh)
  • Imphal (Manipur)
  • Champhai, Darlawn (Mizoram) Less commonly:
  • Road from Ziro to Raga
  • North Vanlaiphai (Mizoram) Rarely:
  • Rest of Meghalaya and Mizoram
  • Arunachal Pradesh / Nagaland border

Parasol leaf tree (Macaranga peltata) is common along the southwestern coast anywhere south of Mumbai and seems to be virtually exclusive to that area, I have yet to find it anywhere else in India. To identify it, look for the teardrop shape of the leaves and the spot where the leaf stem connects to the inner part of the leaf blade.

Recognition:

  • Dense Foliage
  • Shoots drape downwards

Found in:

  • Shimla, Kullu, Manali (Himachal Pradesh)
  • Uttarkashi, Dehradun, Ukhimath (Uttarakhand)
  • to a lesser extent: general area between Dehradun and Ukhimath
  • rarely in Eastern Uttarakhand

Palmyra Palms have a round crown with fan shaped leaves and a trunk with consistent thickness, giving them a lollipop shape.

They appear mostly in 3 areas:

  • Central Bihar
  • Coastal Pondicherry towards Andhra Pradesh/Odisha border + Telangana
  • Around Mumbai

They are also common in

  • coastal states from Tamil Nadu to West Bengal
  • Bihar & Eastern UP
  • Telangana
  • Eastern Gujarat

Recognition:

  • Symmetrical Branches
  • Layered Clusters
  • Clusters shaped like an "inverse function" (see images)
  • narrow, conical, dense foliage

Found in:

  • Jibhi (HP), Chinyalisour, Ukhimath (UK)
  • sometimes Shimla (HP), Range from Dehradun to Rishikesh (UK)
  • rarely remaining UK Mountains; Dharamshala, Palampur, Kullu, Kasol, Manali (HP)
Found in Gujarat, mainly at the southern peninsula (could be fake)
West of Mount Abu, you can find a lot of Euphorbia cacti with flat landscape. Note that this meta is only specific for Rajasthan, Euphorbia appears in other states, like Gujarat, too.

Recognition:

  • Symmetrical Shoots
  • Longer Needles
  • Small shoots make triangular shape
  • Seperated clusteres at different hights

Found in

  • Senge, Manda La (AR)

Recognition:

  • no needles in winter (which is currently all coverage in India with this tree)
  • Conical structure that resembles a christmas tree
  • lighter needles (if present)

Found in:

  • around Senge
  • sometimes around Manda La (both Arunachal Pradesh)

Recognition:

  • needles organized in seperated clumps
  • darker than pines
  • individual branches visible (on high trees)
  • new shoots & many buds often visible from afar
  • Unique branch structure

Extremely rare in India, so far only a singular tree has been found in Manda La.
Teak forests in wet season with boxy car can be found around the Gujarat-Maharashtra border between Surat and Nashik. The trees are quite distinctive, tall and narrow.
If you see a Coconut, hedge in the south eastern half towards Andhra Pradesh, it has more of them.
